planting.note: Plant divisions (pups) after the last frost in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Raja Puri's short, dwarf stature is what lets it fruit within a single warm season even where winter freezes kill the pseudostem back to the ground each year.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after the last frost; Raja Puri is a dwarf, fast-fruiting banana cultivar especially popular with Gulf Coast and Florida home growers because its short 4–7 foot pseudostem reaches flowering size and produces a bunch within one warm growing season — a critical advantage over taller bananas that need more than a year of frost-free growth to reach fruiting size, since a hard freeze that kills the pseudostem each winter resets a tall variety's clock but barely slows a fast, compact grower like Raja Puri. Fruit is medium-small, sweet, and good for fresh eating, borne in bunches lower to the ground than most bananas, which also makes bunches easier to bag and protect from wind damage. Provide consistent moisture and heavy monthly feeding through the growing season, since bananas are fast, heavy feeders. In zone 8b–9, mulch the root zone deeply in fall to protect the rhizome through winter, and expect the pseudostem to die back with hard freezes and resprout from the root system in spring.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Bananas for the Home Landscape

common_name: Namwah Banana (Pisang Awak, Cold-Tolerant Thai Cooking Banana)

planting.note: Plant divisions (pups) after the last frost in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Namwah is widely recommended for the Gulf South for its combination of cold tolerance, disease resistance, and reliable fruiting even after a winter freeze-back.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after the last frost; Namwah, also known as Pisang Awak, is a Thai banana cultivar widely recommended by Gulf South extension programs for home growers because it combines good cold tolerance, resistance to Panama disease and other common banana ailments, and dependable fruiting even in a shortened growing season after winter dieback. The medium-sized fruit has a sweet, slightly tangy flavor good for fresh eating, and the vigorous, disease-resistant plant tends to sucker freely, quickly forming a productive clump. Like other cold-hardy bananas grown in zone 8b–9, expect the pseudostem to die back to the ground in hard freezes and resprout from the root system in spring; mulch heavily over the root zone in fall for extra insulation. Feed heavily and water consistently through the growing season, since bananas are fast-growing, heavy feeders that respond strongly to rich soil and regular moisture.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Bananas for the Home Landscape

planting.note: Plant divisions (pups) after the last frost in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Mysore is an Indian cultivar noted among Southern banana growers for better cold tolerance and more reliable fruit set than many dessert-type bananas.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after the last frost; Mysore is a widely grown Indian banana cultivar valued in Gulf South plantings for better cold tolerance and more consistent fruiting than many purely dessert-type bananas, while still producing sweet, thin-skinned fruit with a pleasant, slightly tart edge good for fresh eating. The clump grows vigorously and suckers readily, and like other cold-tolerant bananas the pseudostem typically dies back to the ground with hard freezes in zone 8b–9 but resprouts from the surviving rhizome in spring, often reaching fruiting size again within a single long growing season. Feed heavily with a balanced, nitrogen-rich fertilizer through the growing season and provide consistent irrigation, since bananas are shallow-rooted, fast-growing plants that suffer quickly under drought stress. Mulch the root zone deeply going into winter for extra cold protection, and thin excess pups to one or two per clump to concentrate energy into fruiting stems.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Bananas for the Home Landscape

planting.note: Plant after the last frost in full sun with a trellis or fence; Incense is a USDA hybrid combining the cold hardiness of native maypop with a more tropical relative for larger, more fragrant flowers, and the roots survive winter to resprout each spring in zone 6–9.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun with a sturdy trellis or fence for climbing; Incense is a USDA hybrid passionflower combining native maypop (Passiflora incarnata) with the more tender South American Passiflora cincinnata, bred to combine maypop's reliable cold-hardiness with larger, showier, more intensely fragrant deep-purple flowers than the straight native species. Like maypop, the vine dies back to the ground in winter through much of its hardiness range and resprouts vigorously from the roots in late spring — do not disturb or remove the crown before new growth appears, as it can be slow to emerge. Flowers are followed by egg-sized, aromatic fruit with sweet-tart pulp similar to tropical passionfruit, though fruit set is often lighter than the straight maypop species; plant more than one vine to improve cross-pollination and fruiting. Incense is also an important larval host plant for Gulf fritillary and variegated fritillary butterflies, adding pollinator-garden value beyond its fruit and ornamental flowers.

common_name: Winkler American Hazelnut (Blight-Resistant Native Hazelnut Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or bare-root plants in spring in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Winkler is a named selection of the native American hazelnut valued for good resistance to Eastern filbert blight, and benefits from a second, genetically distinct hazelnut nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Winkler is a long-cultivated named selection of the native American hazelnut, valued in nut-breeding circles for its strong natural resistance to Eastern filbert blight, the fungal disease that devastates the larger-nutted European hazelnut (Corylus avellana) across much of its Eastern US range. Because of this resistance, Winkler has been widely used as breeding stock for filbert-blight-tolerant hybrid hazelnuts, and it can also be grown directly as a small, multi-stemmed shrub for a reliable, low-input nut crop. Nuts are smaller than European hazelnut but flavorful, ripening in late summer to fall and often eaten by wildlife if not netted or harvested promptly. Like other hazelnuts, Winkler is not self-fertile and needs a second, genetically distinct hazelnut planted nearby for pollination and nut set — wind, not insects, carries the pollen, so plant within about 20 feet for reliable results. The shrub suckers over time to form a multi-stemmed thicket; thin out old wood periodically to keep the planting productive and easy to harvest.
sources: Oregon State University Extension — Hazelnut Breeding
Rutgers New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station — Hazelnut Breeding Program
